1:
Gill and Henry both read the opening as a resumption after a deliberate silence. God had discoursed at length on the works of nature, Gill says, to reconcile Job's mind to his providence, then paused so that Job might answer; finding him silent, he began again. Henry puts it that after heaping up hard questions, to show by Job's ignorance in nature what an incompetent judge he was of providence, God clenches the nail with one demand more; Job being too confounded to speak, God put him upon replying. He adds that this speech is not said to come out of the whirlwind, so some take it for a still small voice, which worked on Job more than the storm had, as it did on Elijah. Clarke agrees from the word itself: answered refers to nothing Job had said and no question asked, but means the Lord continued his discourse; and the man who has made so free with God and his government must answer for what he has heard.

On the question itself the voices differ in where they put the stress. Gill asks whether a man can instruct the God of knowledge, who gives men wisdom in the first place; his answer is that the man who submits to the chastising hand may be instructed by it, while the man who contends is not in the way of instruction at all, the word carrying the sense of chastisement too. Ellicott prefers a different construction, either can he that reproveth contend with the Almighty, or can contending with the Almighty instruct him, glossed as asking whether Job is prepared to go on disputing and whether there is hope of convincing God by argument. Delitzsch reads it as asking whether Job will persist, and makes the term for the man a fault-finder: he who sets God right as though he knew better must answer the questions put to him. Henry hears disdain in it: shall God take instruction from every peevish complainer and change his settled measures to please him? Those who quarrel with God, he says, in effect go about to teach him how to mend his work.

Two of the voices want the passage moved. Clarke thinks it very likely that the first fourteen verses were originally the ending of the poem, and sets out the case he takes from Heath: the former part of the chapter is evidently the conclusion, the latter part is in great disorder, whether through a transcriber's carelessness or, as seems likelier, because the parchment skins of the roll changed places, and the forty-second chapter makes plain that Jehovah is the last speaker. He gives the rearrangement to try: end at the thirty-ninth chapter, go on from the fifteenth verse here into the forty-second, and only then add these fourteen verses. Ellicott knows the proposal and declines it: the transposition would make these verses the climax of the poem and remove the awkwardness of Job resolving to speak no more and then speaking again, but it is unnecessary and has no support from external evidence. Gill finds Job answering with reluctance because obliged to, and offers four senses of his calling himself vile: his arguments shown to have no force, his integrity found wanting in the balance, his distance from God as dust and ashes, which the Greek makes I am nothing, or, as Gill prefers, the vileness of his nature newly seen. Clarke makes it an acknowledgement of inward defilement by a man who cannot excuse himself and must be dumb, confounded at the high thoughts he had entertained of his righteousness. Delitzsch draws the moral from God's manner: he does not demand blind subjection but free submission, and does not extort the acknowledgement of his greatness but effects it by persuasion, proving more forbearing than the friends, those sticklers for their own orthodoxy, who raved against Job.
6:
Why God speaks a second time Gill and Henry answer alike. Gill reports a division over whether the whirlwind had ceased while Job spoke, which would explain his courage, or had grown more boisterous, and takes the second view: comfort does not always follow first convictions, and it was not enough for Job to call himself vile, he must declare his sorrow for sin and own that he had said things he did not understand; so though he had promised to answer no more, God would make him say more. Henry puts it as a rule twice over, that those who profit by what they have heard shall hear more, and that the truly penitent still need to be made more deeply penitent; the convicted must learn not to catch at comfort too soon, since the wound has to be searched to the bottom and not skinned over. Clarke alone treats the renewed challenge as a textual problem, suspecting that this verse and the next were repeated from the opening of the earlier speech and inserted by later hands to join up a wrong gathering of the parchment.

The charge is read as a climax. Delitzsch sets it against the first question and finds the advance: Job had not merely contended with God, wrong as that is, but had gone so far as to lose sight of the divine justice in the government of the world, and, rather than surrender his own righteousness, to doubt God's. Gill takes disannulling the judgment to mean setting one's own judgment against the Lord's, whether his decrees, the sentence gone out of his mouth, or its execution, none of which can be hindered. Clarke hears something harsher, a willingness to condemn God's conduct sooner than be thought in the wrong, which he calls a sort of blasphemy men back into, there being three words hardest of all to pronounce in any language. Ellicott supplies the argument holding the challenge together: God is about to prove Job's inability to govern the world morally from his inability to govern the more formidable animals, so that if he cannot restrain them he will hardly tread down the wicked, and if he cannot hold the wicked in check he can neither protect himself from their fury nor deliver himself out of the hand of God.

Then come the impossible commands, taken as irony with a purpose. Gill has Job told to work himself up into a passion, at least seemingly, putting on the airs of a wrathful king whose wrath is as messengers of death, to see whether such means will humble a proud man. Delitzsch makes it the robing of a subject in the robes of the King of kings, sending his wrath over pride and evil-doing for their complete removal, and reads the word for the overflowings in its proper sense of oversteppings. Henry works through the comparison item by item: man cannot speak with the commanding force of a God who speaks and it is done, one of his thunders overruling all our whispers, and if Job will be compared for majesty he must array himself in all the pomp he has. On hiding the proud in the dust Gill offers the dust of death, an inglorious burial like malefactors thrown into a common pit, or simply alike, none preferred above another. Clarke reads the binding of the faces as the custom of preserving mummies, swathed so closely that not a feature shows, a face painted on the outside while the real face is bound in secret under rollers never meant to be removed. On the last verse Gill and Clarke turn the irony into doctrine: since Job could do none of these things, his right hand could not save him, and he should submit to the hand that could, no man's right hand saving him from temporal evils, much less with an everlasting salvation.
15:
What behemoth is divides the voices sharply. Henry sees no reason to leave the received opinion that the elephant is meant, a creature of larger stature than any other and of such reputation that it could scarcely be omitted from a survey of four-footed beasts, and he frames the description as a question: consider whether you can contend with him who made the beast and gave him his power, or whether it is not wiser to submit. Gill starts from the same received view but will not hold it. He reports that one authority dissents for the river horse, named for its head and said to neigh, then weighs the clauses against the elephant and finds them failing: the strength in the loins agrees badly, the bones are not iron but porous and spongy except the teeth, and the tail, short in both, suits the river horse better for its smoothness and firmness. Clarke clears the ground by showing that the name settles nothing: the Latin keeps the Hebrew word, the Syriac and Arabic too, the Chaldee is indefinite, the Greek gives simply beasts, and an older English version the cruel beast, which he thinks as near the truth as any.

Clarke then goes further than the others will. Critics and naturalists have narrowed the choice to the elephant and the hippopotamus, and on the characters he allows the balance to lie with the hippopotamus; but some parts suit even that animal badly, and he doubts whether any animal now in existence is the one described. With Good he supposes it extinct, and points to three lost genera whose skeletons have been recovered, one the mammoth he had examined himself. Ellicott takes the other available escape, that more than one animal may be meant. The word is the natural plural of a term for domestic cattle, and the description does not seem to answer to one creature: the first six verses would suit the elephant and the last four the hippopotamus. He states the objection to it himself, that the word is used of domestic cattle precisely in contrast with wild beasts and neither animal is domestic, and offers as a further possibility a Coptic word meaning water-ox concealed in the name. Against the hippopotamus he presses two details, that it does not frequent mountains and does not exactly eat grass like an ox. Delitzsch leaves the identification alone and settles the form: the plural carries no numerical force, playing the part of an abstract ending, so the word denotes the beast as such, the giant among beasts.

On the particulars the sources supply learning rather than decide. Ellicott corrects three renderings in as many verses: sinews for the navel, thighs for the word the older version left coarse, and tubes for the strong pieces of brass. Gill gathers what can be found about the tail: one traveller made the elephant's four hands long while the river horse has a short twisted tail like a boar's, and one commentator takes the verb to mean maketh to stand, stiff as a cedar. On the bones he collects testimonies to the hardness of hippopotamus teeth, valued above ivory and harder to work. The claim that the creature is chief of the ways of God divides them again. Gill allows it either as the beginning of God's works, which would make the river horse earlier than the elephant by a day of creation, or as a superiority limited to its own kind, since man is chief of all God's works. Ellicott thinks the title fits the elephant better, for its intelligence and usefulness, and reports three ways of taking the obscure clause that follows: that only his Maker can bring a sword near him, that his Maker furnished him with his sword, or that whoever would dress him for meat may try it. He prefers a combination of the first and last.
20:
The pasture on the mountains is where Clarke closes the case. It cannot be the hippopotamus, he argues, since that animal is seldom found far from its rivers; the creature described frequents the places where prey is thickest and makes a mock of the beasts of the field, which can neither resist its power nor escape its agility, all of which answers to the mammoth and not at all to the river horse. Gill lets the verse tell against neither, since grass grows on mountains and feeds the river horse as well as the elephant, and a creature needing that much could be supplied from nowhere smaller; what strikes him is the marvel that a beast bred in a river should come out to find food on a mountain. He supports it from a northern animal, the sea morss, about the size of an ox with a head like one, two long teeth standing out of the upper jaw, and a hide an inch thick that no lance will enter, which climbs from the sea to the mountain tops by its teeth to feed on grass. Delitzsch leaves the animal and works on the shade it lies in, identifying the tree as the wild lote, found in Syria and Egypt and through Africa, and citing the poets for the beasts of the steppe seeking its cover.

On the lying down the voices divide again along the same line. Ellicott judges that if the description applies to one animal at all, the shade suits the elephant better, and adds a caution about how the question has been argued: the critics' judgment has been biased by what they assume about where the book was written, on the supposition that its author would know the river-horse of Egypt sooner than the elephant of India, though elephants abound in Africa too. Gill reads it the other way, since the elephant is reported to sleep standing and to lie down rarely, finding it troublesome to rise again, and is described by some as taller than the trees, so the shade fits the river horse better. Clarke declines to decide, saying only that these verses refer to habits with which we are and must be unacquainted, while allowing that the willows of the brook would agree well enough with the hippopotamus.

The river comes last, read as understatement rather than hyperbole. Gill reports what the philosophers allowed the elephant for thirst, nine bushels at a feeding and more at noon, but thinks drinking up a river too great an hyperbole, preferring to render it that though a river press on him with all its force he neither hurries out nor is frightened, which suits the river horse proceeding through the stream unconcerned, lifting his head now and then to breathe, where the elephant cannot wade deeper than his trunk. Ellicott renders it to the same effect, that if a river is violent he does not tremble but is confident though Jordan swell up to his mouth. Clarke takes it as a figure of unstoppable course, no river staying him, and from the naming of Jordan infers that the creature once inhabited the mountains and marshes of Palestine. Gill reads the taking as a question, whether men can take him before his eyes, and answers that neither animal is taken openly but by craft, both being trapped in covered pits. Clarke ends by committing himself: this is the mastodon or mammoth or some such creature, made as the chief of God's works, shown in various countries for a time and then cut off, its skeletons preserved so that later ages might see the power that produced it and admire the providence that ended a race which would otherwise have extinguished every other. He has read all that the chief of learned men wrote for the hippopotamus, and remains convinced the animal is extinct now.
